title: Transverse and longitudinal waves
prior_knowledge_summary: A progressive wave transfers energy while points in the medium oscillate locally about equilibrium.
Frequency, wavelength and wave speed describe different features of a progressive wave.
The wave equation v = fλ links wave speed, frequency and wavelength when units are compatible.
new_learning: Compare particle displacement direction with energy-transfer direction.
Identify compressions and rarefactions as features of a longitudinal wave.
not_yet_taught: interpretation of displacement-distance and displacement-time graphs for transverse or longitudinal waves
wave intensity and its relationships with power, area or amplitude

blocks.heading: The disturbance goes forward, but which way does the material move?
content: Send a pulse along a rope by flicking one end upward. The pulse moves across the room, yet a coloured mark on the rope moves mainly up and down. Now push and pull the end of a spring. The crowded regions move along the spring, while one marked coil moves back and forth.
Both arrangements transfer energy away from the hand. The difference is the angle between local particle displacement and the direction of energy transfer.

figure.purpose: Create the classification puzzle by contrasting two local motions with the same forward energy transfer.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper teacher sketch split into two physical scenes. Left: a rope pulse travels right while one coloured rope mark moves vertically. Right: a spring disturbance travels right while one coloured coil moves horizontally. Use short arrows only and do not name either wave type.
figure.alt_text: A rope mark moves across the travel direction while a spring coil moves along the travel direction.

blocks.heading: Always compare two directions
content: First identify the direction in which the disturbance and energy travel. Then identify the displacement direction of one particle or point in the medium. Classification comes from comparing those two directions, not from the visible shape alone.
A useful test is to draw two arrows at one marked particle. One arrow is for energy transfer. The other is for particle displacement. Ask whether the arrows are at right angles or parallel.
The particle displacement may reverse during an oscillation. Its line of motion still has the same relationship to the energy-transfer direction.

figure.purpose: Teach the two-arrow classification routine without relying on wave shape.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper direction card showing a fixed rightward energy-transfer arrow and two alternative particle-motion double arrows: vertical and horizontal. Mark the right angle on the vertical case and parallel guide lines on the horizontal case. Keep wave-type names covered by question marks.
figure.alt_text: A direction card compares particle motion perpendicular or parallel to rightward energy transfer.

blocks.heading: Transverse means perpendicular
content: Definition to learn: a transverse wave is a wave in which the displacement of particles is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
On the rope, energy travels horizontally while a marked point is displaced vertically. The two directions are perpendicular, so the rope wave is transverse.
A ripple travelling across water can also make a small floating marker move mostly up and down while energy spreads across the surface. Again, compare local displacement with energy transfer.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: a wave in which the displacement of particles is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer

figure.purpose: Anchor the controlled transverse definition to two physical examples.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper comparison sketch with a rope mark and a floating water marker. In each, show a rightward energy arrow and a vertical double-headed displacement arrow with a clear right-angle symbol. Label the relationship perpendicular and the classification transverse.
figure.alt_text: Rope and water examples show particle displacement perpendicular to energy transfer.

blocks.heading: Longitudinal means parallel
content: Definition to learn: a longitudinal wave is a wave in which particle displacement is parallel to the direction of energy propagation.

Push and pull a spring along its length. Each coil oscillates back and forth along the spring while the disturbance and energy travel along the spring. The directions are parallel, so the wave is longitudinal.

Sound in air works in the same directional way. An air particle oscillates back and forth along the line in which sound energy travels. The air particle does not travel from the source to the listener.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: a wave in which particle displacement is parallel to the direction of energy propagation

figure.purpose: Anchor the controlled longitudinal definition to spring and sound examples.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper comparison sketch with a spring coil and a row of air particles. Show rightward energy arrows and horizontal double-headed particle-displacement arrows on the same line. Label the relationship parallel and the classification longitudinal.
figure.alt_text: Spring and sound examples show particle displacement parallel to energy propagation.

blocks.heading: Read compressions and rarefactions physically
content: As a longitudinal disturbance passes through a spring, some regions have coils closer together than their normal spacing. These crowded regions are compressions. Regions where coils are farther apart are rarefactions.
A compression is not one fixed group of coils travelling together. Each coil oscillates locally. The region of reduced spacing advances as neighbouring coils take part.
For sound in air, a compression is a region where particles are more crowded, and a rarefaction is a region where they are less crowded. Both regions travel with the wave pattern.

figure.purpose: Connect compression and rarefaction labels to actual particle spacing without introducing graphs.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper physical spring sketch with one tightly spaced region and one widely spaced region. Label compression and rarefaction, mark normal spacing faintly, show one coil's short back-and-forth arrow and a separate rightward pattern-travel arrow.
figure.alt_text: A spring has a compression with close coils and a rarefaction with widely spaced coils.

blocks.heading: Do not classify a wave by its drawn shape
content: It feels natural to call any wavy line transverse because the line rises and falls. That shortcut fails because a drawing may be a graph, a pattern, or only a way to show changing values. The wave type depends on physical particle displacement relative to energy transfer.

A longitudinal sound wave is sometimes drawn as a smooth curve, but its air particles still oscillate parallel to the travel direction. A rope may look momentarily straight as a pulse passes, but its marked points can still move perpendicular to energy transfer.
Use the two-arrow test: identify energy transfer, identify particle displacement, then compare their directions. Detailed graph reading belongs to the next lesson.

figure.purpose: Replace shape-based classification with the directional test while preserving the L6 graph boundary.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper misconception panel. Cross out a speech bubble saying wavy line means transverse. Beside it, show the two-arrow test applied to a physical rope point and physical air particle. Include a small locked graph icon labelled next lesson, with no axes or graph interpretation.
figure.alt_text: A misconception panel rejects shape-based classification and uses particle and energy directions instead.

blocks.heading: One decision route for both wave types
content: Track one particle, not the travelling pattern. Mark the direction of its displacement and the direction of energy transfer.
Perpendicular directions mean transverse. Parallel directions mean longitudinal. In a longitudinal wave, identify crowded regions as compressions and spread-out regions as rarefactions.
In both types, particles oscillate locally while energy is transferred. Wave speed may still be found from v = fλ when frequency and wavelength are known, but speed does not decide the wave type.

figure.purpose: Summarise classification, physical longitudinal features and the distinction between speed and type.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper decision map. Start with two direction arrows, branch to perpendicular and transverse or parallel and longitudinal. Under longitudinal add physical compression and rarefaction particle strips. Add a separate small v = f lambda card labelled speed, not type.
figure.alt_text: A decision map classifies waves from direction and separates wave speed from wave type.

misconceptions_addressed: The visible shape alone determines whether a wave is transverse.
Particles travel with compressions from source to receiver.
Wave speed determines the wave type.
